description_full: The Manitowoc Company, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides engineered lifting solutions in the Americas, Europe, Africa, the Middle East, the Asia Pacific, and internationally. The company designs, manufactures, and distributes crawler-mounted lattice-boom cranes under the Manitowoc brand; a line of top-slewing and self-erecting tower cranes under the Potain brand; mobile hydraulic cranes comprising rough-terrain cranes, all-terrain cranes, truck-mounted cranes, telescopic crawler cranes, industrial cranes, and hydraulic boom trucks under the Grove, Shuttlelift, and National Crane brands. It also provides aftermarket services, such as sale of parts and accessories, field service work, routine maintenance services, technical support, erection and decommissioning services, crane and component remanufacturing, training, and telematics services. The company's crane products are used in various applications, including energy production/distribution and utilities; petrochemical and industrial; infrastructure, such as road, bridge, and airport construction; and commercial and residential construction. It serves various customers, including dealers, rental companies, contractors, and government entities in the petrochemical, industrial, commercial construction, power and utilities, infrastructure, and residential construction end markets. The Manitowoc Company, Inc. was founded in 1902 and is headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

financial_summary: Manitowoc Company, Inc. (The) is a small-cap industrials business with a $860M market cap on $2.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and -4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 3% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 18% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The company is burning through $15M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 1.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 4.8% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 2% operating margin trails the Industrials median (9%) by 6pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.22x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-4.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 95% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 55% and a beta of 1.23, it amplifies market moves.
About $8.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 58% in the 2020 crash, 61% in the 2022 bear market and 95% in 2008.
val: Multiples send mixed signals against Industrials peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 9.0 vs 13.4, richer on P/E 33.5 vs 24.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 103% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -1.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $17.50 on average, 27% below the price.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.4%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.85).
It runs a 18% gross margin and burns cash (FCF margin -1%).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.08x.
ROE of 1% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.5% of revenue on R&D and 0.4% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.4x net debt to EBITDA ($77.3M of cash against $460.8M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.4x.
Working capital ties up about 134 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.3% over 3 years, 9.2% over 5 years and -4.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 19%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 3.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (1.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.8%, and institutions hold 87%.
The share count has grown 0.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 4,700 employees, each generates about $477K of revenue, 1.3x the Industrials median, and revenue has fallen 2.2% a year across its filed history.
Free cash flow is negative, at -$3K per employee.
CEO pay is $1.9M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
